findings.source_text: monarchy being lure Divino, which we never heard of
findings.candidate_text: monarchy being jure divino — by divine right — which we never heard of
findings.problem: OCR 'lure Divino' is correctly fixed to jure divino, but the gloss 'by divine right' is the candidate's own addition. Locke gives no English here.
findings.suggested_fix: monarchy being jure divino, which we never heard of (or keep the gloss if the edition adopts a policy that allows helper glosses)

findings.source_text: though, caeteris paribus, they commonly prefer the heir
findings.candidate_text: Other things being equal (caeteris paribus), they commonly prefer the heir
findings.problem: The candidate added an English gloss that Locke did not supply and moved the Latin into parentheses after it, which makes Locke's Latin look secondary.
findings.suggested_fix: Other things being equal, they commonly prefer ... (or: Caeteris paribus, they commonly prefer ...)

findings.source_text: the original of governments, as they have begun de facto
findings.candidate_text: the origins of governments as they have actually begun, de facto
findings.problem: 'actually' duplicates the Latin as an added gloss that Locke did not supply.
findings.suggested_fix: the origins of governments as they have begun de facto

findings.source_text: to begin a new one, in vacuis locis, in any part of the world, they can find free and unpossessed
findings.candidate_text: to begin a new one, in vacuis locis — in any part of the world they can find free and unoccupied
findings.problem: The dash makes Locke's own following phrase read as a gloss of the Latin. Locke arguably meant it that way, so no content is added, but the punctuation now explicitly presents it as a translation.
findings.suggested_fix: in vacuis locis, in any part of the world they can find free and unoccupied

findings.source_text: amor sceleratus habendi, evil concupiscence
findings.candidate_text: amor sceleratus habendi — evil craving for possession —
findings.problem: Locke supplies his own gloss 'evil concupiscence'. The candidate replaced it with a closer translation of the Latin ('for possession' renders habendi), so the gloss is now the candidate's rather than Locke's modernized.
findings.suggested_fix: amor sceleratus habendi — evil greed — (a modernized 'concupiscence' without adding 'possession'), or keep as is

findings.source_text: America, which is still a pattern of the first ages in Asia and Europe, whilst the inhabitants were too few for the country, ... are little more than generals
findings.candidate_text: (America is still a pattern of the first ages in Asia and Europe, when the inhabitants were too few for the country, and the lack of people and money gave men no temptation ...)
findings.problem: In Locke the 'whilst' clause can be read as the condition under which the kings are little more than generals. The candidate places it inside a parenthesis attached only to 'the first ages', which settles an ambiguous clause in one direction and takes it away from the main claim about the kings. The shift is small but real.
findings.suggested_fix: So we see that the kings of the Indians in America (which is still a pattern of the first ages in Asia and Europe), while the inhabitants were too few for the country and the lack of people and money gave men no temptation to enlarge their holdings of land or fight over wider territory, are little more than generals of their armies.

summary: No major findings in chapters 8-11. Sampled paragraphs keep every clause, example, hedge and citation. The Hooker, Acosta, Justin and Scripture passages are complete, with correct footnote markers and citation form. The known source defects (lure Divino, 'thought [fit]', four truncated last paragraphs, Hooker's 'sith' printed as 'such', the '1.'/'l.' OCR) are all correctly repaired and match raw.txt. The candidate added English glosses to Latin in three places (jure divino, caeteris paribus, de facto) and rewrote Locke's own gloss of amor sceleratus habendi. The other minor points are a parenthesis in ch8 p16 that settles an ambiguous 'whilst' clause and one residual inverted Hooker sentence (ch11 p1). The whole-chapter term scan is clean: every 'possessions' matches Locke's own word, and there are no hits for legislature, natural state, state of warfare or residual archaisms.
